scrollSteps.value: Our teenage sapphic yearning was analog and lonely.

We grew up before the internet let us find our people and curate our entertainment. And in our Southern, culturally conservative communities, we didn’t always have safe access to media that could help us make sense of our otherness. So we consumed the same popular culture as our peers, from watching the same handful of heavily edited movies that rotated through TNT, TBS and USA (Tommy Boy, anyone?) to sprinting to the TV after school to watch Total Request Live. And this media and the people in it were mostly heterosexual.

In the absence of mainstream queer icons, we each found ourselves drawn to examples of otherness in the media. We unconsciously clocked gay subtext and made it the main story: the powerful women of the budding WNBA, that kiss between two seemingly “straight” girls in Cruel Intentions, a strong affinity for Queen Latifah during her Living Single days.

Individually, we held onto these moments because it made us feel less unusual as we figured out the people  we were supposed to become. It took us almost 20 years to realize that we’d spent the 90s and early aughts on parallel pop culture treasure hunts — and discovered many of the same queer-ish treasures.

Ashleé and Jan first met around 2025 at Western Kentucky University’s student newspaper. Neither of us had fully acknowledged our queerness: Jan was closeted in high school because she was still figuring out her sexuality and was terrified of the negative impact that coming out would have on the people she respected. Ashleé grew up knowing she was different, but was unable to put a name on the flutters she felt when certain women popped up on her TV. And as an adult, the bounds of compulsory heterosexuality sucked out the space for her to imagine life as gay woman.

By the time we reconnected in our 30s, Jan was out and married to a woman. Ashleé was divorced from a man and identified as queer. Yet as our paths to discovering and nurturing our queerness diverged, we could still point to the same pivotal moments in popular culture that served as breadcrumbs to our own self discoveries. We call these queernections — moments in which we identified with and attached meaning to the same covert and overt queer media, characters and moments in popular culture during the early stages of our coming out journey. Discovering that we shared so many queernections has been a balm for our younger, insecure selves, because the truth is that we might have been lonely in our otherness, but we were never really alone.
This is our journey. Maybe you can see yourself in it, too.

timelineInstructions.value: Each side of this timeline shows a personal journey: Jan’s on the left, and Ashleé’s on the right.

The rainbow lines represent overarching themes to our queernections, and the dots are events within those themes. Use the rainbow dots at the top as reminders of the theme’s definition as you move down the page.

When the rainbow lines push in toward the center, that means that either Jan or Ashleé experienced a queernection at this cultural touchpoint. On the right is Ashleé’s first touchpoint: Kelly Kapowski on Saved by the Bell. Each touchpoint can be attached to multiple themes, or none at all — that’s why these touchpoints appear on Jan’s side along the black line.
When the lines with the same theme collide in the center, that’s a queernection! Here, both Jan and Ashleé felt a Girl Power connection with Lori "Ice" Fetrick on American Gladiators.

Tap any circle with a plus sign to add it to your own personal queer canon list, and tap any circle with an x to remove it. You can manage your list in the events drawer at the bottom. We’ll use this to show the all your queernections later.
